findings: Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

general.summary: No directly applicable, high-quality evidence was retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

Culture: no growth to date. Elevated protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation). Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: 1. No epidural hematoma, epidural abscess or fluid collection at the spinal anesthesia site. 2. Mild gadolinium enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots bilaterally. 3. No intrinsic spinal cord signal abnormality and no cord compression. 4. Cervical spine normal.
Bedside respiratory function 8 h after admission: FVC 2.4 L (75% predicted; 39 mL/kg at 61 kg) L. MIP -42 cmH2O L. MEP 58 cmH2O L. Change: FVC 2.6 L to 2.4 L over 8 h (8% fall). Cough effective.

findings: Sinus rhythm 68-116 bpm, sinus tachycardia most of the recording
output.impression: 24-hour continuous telemetry. Sinus tachycardia most of the recording (range 68-116 bpm). One episode of postural hypotension (88/60 mmHg on sitting up). No pauses and no arrhythmia.
output.rhythm_summary: Sinus rhythm with sinus tachycardia most of the recording.

interactions: IVIg and ibuprofen: NSAIDs add to the risk of IVIg-associated renal impairment; regular NSAID use is avoided during the infusion course and hydration maintained (relative caution).
IVIg and ferrous sulfate: no interaction identified.
output.proposed: IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days in a breastfeeding patient taking ferrous sulfate and ibuprofen as needed
warnings: Lactation: immune globulin is a normal component of breast milk and IVIg is considered acceptable during breastfeeding; ferrous sulfate and ibuprofen are compatible with breastfeeding (LactMed).
IVIg: headache, aseptic meningitis, renal impairment and thrombosis are recognised adverse effects (IVIg SmPC); the postpartum period adds to thrombotic risk.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Polyradiculoneuropathy pattern (demyelinating or axonal features, absent F-waves, sural sparing where present); may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Nerve conduction studies establish the polyradiculoneuropathy and its demyelinating pattern, which a spinal anaesthetic injury does not produce [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Albuminocytological dissociation: raised protein with cells <5/mm3 (5-50/mm3 compatible but prompts an alternative; >50/mm3 suggests another diagnosis); protein may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein and glucose
action_criteria.rationale: CSF supports the diagnosis and excludes infection after neuraxial anaesthesia [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No epidural haematoma, abscess or cord lesion; nerve root enhancement may be seen
action_criteria.label: Optional contrast spine MRI to exclude an epidural haematoma, abscess or cauda equina lesion after spinal anaesthesia
action_criteria.rationale: Recent spinal anaesthesia with leg-predominant weakness and sensory symptoms raises a neuraxial complication; without back pain, fever or sphincter dysfunction the scan is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Baseline values before treatment; abnormal liver tests or low albumin mark a higher risk of a severe course; no metabolic or toxic alternative
action_criteria.label: Baseline blood tests: full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, liver tests, albumin, glucose and CK
action_criteria.rationale: Routine blood tests exclude metabolic mimics and give the baseline before IVIg [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC in L, % predicted and mL/kg, MIP and MEP, with the trend; ICU-level monitoring if FVC <20 mL/kg or <60% predicted, MIP weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O, a fall of more than 30%, or bulbar weakness with weak cough
action_criteria.label: Bedside respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP), repeated serially while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: She is still progressing and cannot stand; serial FVC, MIP and MEP, read against her weight, decide when ICU-level monitoring is needed [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous telemetry with blood pressure monitoring: sinus tachycardia to 116 bpm and one episode of postural hypotension (88/60 mmHg) in the first 24 hours; autonomic instability (rate and blood pressure lability, bradyarrhythmia) requires continued monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.label: Continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction is common in GBS and can cause bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability; monitoring continues while weakness progresses [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus tachycardia 108 bpm with normal intervals (QTc 432 ms) and no conduction or ST-T abnormality: a baseline while autonomic involvement can still develop
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline 12-lead ECG screens for autonomic dysrhythmia and conduction abnormality and gives the QTc before treatment [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ibuprofen adds to IVIg renal risk; IVIg and her current medicines are compatible with breastfeeding
action_criteria.label: Check ferrous sulfate and ibuprofen against IVIg and breastfeeding before IVIg
action_criteria.rationale: An as-needed NSAID and lactation are the concrete issues; neither delays treatment, so the check is recommended rather than required (ROUND_POLICY ruling 6).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on immunotherapy in GBS; not needed for the diagnosis or the treatment decision
action_criteria.label: Optional literature search on GBS treatment in the postpartum period
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not attribute the weakness to the spinal anaesthetic: symmetric weakness of all four limbs progressing over 2 weeks with areflexia does not fit a neuraxial injury.
required_recommendations: Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 24 g/day at 61 kg) now: she cannot stand (GBS disability score 4) and weakness began about 2 weeks ago; plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative [EAN_PNS_2023].

Admit to a monitored bed with FVC, MIP and MEP every 4-6 hours (FVC already 2.6 to 2.4 L); move to ICU-level monitoring if FVC falls below 60% predicted or 20 mL/kg (about 1.2 L at 61 kg), MIP becomes weaker than -40 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O, FVC falls by more than 30%, bulbar weakness appears, or blood pressure and heart rate become unstable [EAN_PNS_2023, Lawn_2001].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while weakness progresses; postural precautions for the orthostatic hypotension.
Breastfeeding can continue during IVIg; review each co-medication, including any analgesic for neuropathic pain, for lactation safety [LactMed].
Pharmacological DVT prophylaxis (low-molecular-weight heparin, compatible with breastfeeding): she is postpartum and immobile.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy), postpartum

differential.diagnosis: Spinal anaesthesia-related neuropathy / cauda equina injury or epidural complication
differential.key_features: Neuraxial injury is restricted to one or a few roots and appears within days; here weakness is symmetric, ascending, involves the hands, and the contrast spine MRI shows no haematoma, abscess or collection.
Pregnancy and the postpartum period are also linked to CIDP onset; progression over 2 weeks fits GBS. Reassess if worsening continues beyond 8 weeks.
Subacute and length-dependent; does not cause weakness progressing over 2 weeks with CSF albuminocytological dissociation and demyelinating conduction.
Asymmetric mononeuropathy multiplex; symmetric ascending pattern and demyelinating NCS argue against.

key_clinical_evidence: Distal latencies of 7.4-8.8 ms and conduction velocities of 24-28 m/s in the leg nerves are demyelinating; low distal CMAP amplitudes alone do not make the study axonal [EAN_PNS_2023].
Weakness is leg-predominant but the hands are mildly weak and the arm reflexes reduced, so the required bilateral limb features are met; no infectious antecedent is needed in the postpartum setting.
Spinal anaesthesia-related neuropathy is anatomically restricted and early; the symmetric ascending presentation 2 weeks later, with a normal spine MRI apart from root enhancement, does not fit.
IVIg is compatible with breastfeeding; immune globulin is a normal component of breast milk [LactMed].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anaesthetic injuries are anatomically restricted and present within days; the symmetric ascending weakness 1-2 weeks after surgery, with hand involvement and a spine MRI without haematoma or abscess, is GBS.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent spinal anaesthesia 22 days before presentation, with leg tingling at discharge
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a direct anaesthetic injury or epidural complication rather than an autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy.

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 108. Normal QTc (432 ms). No acute ST-T wave changes.

labs.interpretation: Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (low). CRP 6.8 mg/L and ESR 42 mm/hr (elevated). Remaining values within reference ranges.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

findings.finding: DML 7.4 ms (prolonged); CV 28 m/s (severely reduced); CMAP 1.2 mV (markedly reduced)
DML 8.8 ms (prolonged); CV 24 m/s (severely reduced); CMAP 0.8 mV (markedly reduced)
DML 4.6 ms (mildly prolonged); CV 50 m/s (low normal); CMAP 6.2 mV
Absent bilateral posterior tibial and peroneal; median minimum latency prolonged (33 ms)
Tibialis anterior, medial gastrocnemius and vastus lateralis bilaterally: markedly reduced recruitment; no fibrillation potentials. First dorsal interosseous: mildly reduced recruitment

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL study. 1. Severely prolonged distal motor latencies and conduction velocities of 24-28 m/s in bilateral posterior tibial and peroneal motor nerves, with markedly reduced distal CMAP amplitudes (0.8-1.2 mV). 2. Mildly prolonged median distal motor latency and prolonged median F-wave latency. 3. Absent sural sensory responses bilaterally; reduced median sensory amplitudes (8 µV). 4. Absent lower limb F-waves and H-reflexes. 5. Markedly reduced recruitment in leg muscles without denervation. Pattern consistent with a demyelinating sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy, lower limb predominant.

quantitative_data.pattern: Demyelinating sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy, lower limb predominant, with mild upper limb involvement

metadata.difficulty_description: Postpartum GBS with spinal anaesthesia as a confounder: surgical complications must be excluded and the demyelinating NCS read despite low distal CMAPs
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions (NCS/EMG, CSF, baseline labs, respiratory function, telemetry), optional spine MRI, recommended interaction and lactation check, 1 red herring (spinal anaesthesia).
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral leg weakness over 2 weeks, unable to walk, 22 days after emergency cesarean section under spinal anesthesia.

past_medical_history: G1P1, emergency cesarean section 22 days ago (38 weeks, fetal distress)

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. P. is a 29-year-old primiparous woman presenting 22 days after an emergency lower-segment cesarean section performed under spinal anesthesia at 38 weeks for fetal distress. She was discharged on postoperative day 5 with mild bilateral lower limb numbness and tingling, which was attributed to residual effects of spinal anesthesia. Starting approximately 8 days after surgery, she noticed progressive bilateral leg weakness, which spread from distal to proximal over the following two weeks. She could initially perform daily activities with assistance, but is now completely unable to stand or support herself. She reports burning and tingling in both lower extremities extending to mid-thigh. Over the last few days she has also found it harder to fasten buttons and grip a cup. There is no bowel or bladder dysfunction. She denies dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, or visual changes. There was no preceding respiratory illness or diarrheal illness identified. There is no prior history of neuropathy or neurological disease. She has no fever or back pain. She is breastfeeding and is concerned about her ability to care for her newborn.

neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot assess lower limbs. Upper limbs: finger-nose intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No facial weakness. No ptosis. No ophthalmoplegia.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented, anxious about infant care.
neurological_exam.motor: Severe bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 2/5, knee extension 0/5, ankle dorsiflexion 0/5; cannot lift legs off bed. Upper extremity: shoulder abduction 5/5, elbow flexion 5/5, finger abduction 4/5 and grip 4/5 bilaterally (grip about 80% of normal).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral patellar and Achilles. Reduced bilateral biceps and brachioradialis (1+). Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral burning and tingling lower extremities extending to mid-thigh. Reduced pinprick and light touch below mid-calf bilaterally. Vibration reduced at ankles.
